tip: Fronting the object 'een goedkoop hotel' triggers verb-second: 'hebben' lands before the subject 'wij'.
Meenemen is separable: the prefix 'mee' moves to the sentence end, leaving 'neem' in second place.
For 'behind himself' Dutch uses the reflexive 'zich', not 'hem': 'achter zich'.
Proberen connects to a following verb with 'te': 'proberen ... te komen'.
Here 'voor' marks a deadline, meaning 'by Friday', not 'in front of': 'voor vrijdag'.
'Niet' follows the time word: it is 'vandaag niet', not 'niet vandaag'.
'Wel' is the positive counter to 'niet', affirming what was just denied.
'Pas' means 'not until' or 'only then': 'pas ... als je achttien bent'.
Uittrekken is separable: the prefix 'uit' moves to the end: 'trekt ... uit'.
Dutch negates a noun with 'geen', not 'niet': 'geen wifi' = no wifi.
'Vanwege' means 'because of' and takes a noun ('het weer'); 'omdat' would need a full clause.
Dutch asks the time with 'hoe laat', literally 'how late': 'hoe laat het is'.
An adjective can stand alone as a noun: 'de langzame' = the slow one, with 'trein' left out.
Fixed phrase 'zich zorgen maken over' = to worry about: 'maakt zich zorgen over'.
'Per se' (from Latin) means absolutely or no matter what: 'hij wil per se'.
'Hoeven' means 'have to' only in the negative, and pairs with 'te': 'hoeft niet ... te komen'.
Dutch says 'ongelijk hebben' for 'to be wrong', literally 'have wrong': 'ik ongelijk had'.
'Sinds' = since, marking the start point of an ongoing situation: 'sinds mijn vijfde'.
'Zich schamen voor' = to be ashamed of; the reflexive 'zich' is required: 'schaamt zich voor'.
